cues.text: Let us turn now to innovation management frameworks, the fourth chapter of this study session.
Innovation management is the systematic way an organisation generates, evaluates, develops, implements and measures ideas.
Notice that this is a full cycle.
It is not only about having a creative idea; it is about deciding which ideas deserve resources, turning them into something real, and then checking whether they worked.
Innovation management also has to balance two kinds of work.
The first is exploratory work, which means searching for new possibilities.
The second is exploitation of established capabilities, which means getting more value from what the organisation already does well.
Keep that balance in mind, because we will return to it at the end of this chapter.
Now let us look at five frameworks.
The accompanying table sets them out, and I will walk through it row by row.
The columns are: Framework, Mechanism, Best use, and Limitation.
First row: Stage-gate.
Its mechanism is stages separated by review decisions.
Its best use is in capital-intensive or high-risk programmes, where a mistake is expensive.
Its limitation is that it can become bureaucratic.
Second row: Design thinking.
Its mechanism is five steps: empathise, define, ideate, prototype and test.
Its best use is where user needs are unclear.
Its limitation is that a prototype does not prove business viability.
A prototype may show that people like something, but it does not show that the business can earn enough from it.
Third row: Lean startup.
Its mechanism is build, measure, learn, using a minimum viable product, or MVP, and validated learning.
Its best use is where product-market fit is uncertain, meaning you do not yet know whether a market wants what you are offering.
Its limitation is that weak experiments can mislead.
Fourth row: Open innovation.
Its mechanism is partnering and exchanging knowledge externally.
Its best use is to access scarce capabilities that you do not have inside the organisation.
Its limitations are risks around intellectual property, coordination and trust.
Fifth row: Agile innovation.
Its mechanism is iterative increments and feedback.
Its best use is where requirements are evolving.
Its limitation is that it needs prioritisation and discipline.
Let us take each framework in more depth, starting with stage-gate.
A typical stage-gate process has these stages: discovery, scoping, business case, development, testing and validation, and launch.
Between stages sits a gate, which is a review point.
At each gate, leaders make one of four decisions: go, hold, revise or stop.
Go means proceed to the next stage.
Hold means pause the project.
Revise means send it back for changes.
Stop means end it.
This is how stage-gate preserves investment discipline: money is released step by step, and only when the evidence justifies it.
The source also stresses that agile teams can work within stages, and that these frameworks are not mutually exclusive.
An organisation can combine them.
Next, design thinking.
It begins with observing customers rather than assuming their needs.
After observation, you define a problem statement, then generate options, then make low-cost prototypes, and then test them.
Consider the example of a farmer.
The farmer may need weather alerts delivered through low-bandwidth channels, rather than a feature-heavy smartphone dashboard.
The right approach is to prototype both options and observe how the farmer actually uses them.
Observation, not assumption, settles the question.
Remember the limitation, though: even a well-tested prototype does not prove that the business case is viable.
Now lean startup.
Here, a business idea is treated as a hypothesis, something to be tested rather than assumed true.
An MVP is the smallest useful experiment that tests a critical assumption.
It is not a badly engineered production service; it is an experiment, designed to teach you something.
The loop is build, measure and learn.
If the evidence contradicts your model, you pivot, meaning you change direction.
If the evidence supports it, you persevere.
Use meaningful metrics rather than vanity metrics such as raw downloads, which can look impressive while telling you nothing about real value.
And recall the limitation: weak experiments can mislead.
Open innovation can include several forms of partnership: university partnerships, suppliers, startups, hackathons and licensing.
Whatever form you choose, you should define the intellectual property and data sharing arrangements, because those are exactly where the risks of IP, coordination and trust arise.
Finally, the source distinguishes four types of innovation.
Product innovation changes offerings.
Process innovation improves production or delivery.
Business model innovation changes how value is created and captured.
Organisational innovation changes structures and practices.
Incremental improvements and radical bets can coexist in a portfolio.
So an organisation does not have to choose between small steady gains and bold new moves; it can hold both.
This is where our opening balance returns.
Manage exploration with controlled experimentation, and manage exploitation with operational excellence.
Exploration is kept safe through small, controlled tests, while exploitation is sustained through running the existing business very well.
